newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq investigates attempt on Uday.
newsitem.headline: Iraq investigates attempt on Uday.

text.p: Iraqi authorities are investigating the attempt to kill President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, official media reported on Friday, wishing him a quick recovery from his wounds which were said to be not serious.

The ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra published the text of a presidential statement issued hours after Uday, 32, was shot and wounded while driving through al-Mansour, Baghdad's smartest district.
"Wishes for the speedy recovery of Mr Uday after being subjected to a cowardly and treacherous aggression," said al- Thawra on its front page.
No details were given of the identity of the attackers or whether there were other casualties. Investigations were under way, al-Thawra said.
Al-Iraq newspaper said Uday's condition was not worrying and he was in Baghdad's Ibn Sina hospital.
Uday used to drive without bodyguards in Baghdad and many people have reported seeing him alone or with friends dining in Baghdad restaurants.

News on the attempt on Uday's life was first broadcast on Shebab television, a popular channel he owns. A gloomy broadcaster interrupted a programme to announce that Uday was shot and wounded and taken to hospital.

"An official spokesman for the presidential office announced that Mr Uday Saddam Hussein, chairman of the Iraqi Olympic Committee, was subjected tonight to a cowardly attack during which he was wounded at 7 p.m. (1600 GMT)," the station said.
State radio and televion were broadcasting as normal on Friday and life in Baghdad went on as usual with thousands of Moslem worshippers heading for mosques to pray and listen to Friday sermons.
It was the first attempt on Uday's life reported by official Iraqi media.
Uday heads Iraq's National Olympic Committee and is also head of the Iraq Soccer Federation. He owns Iraq's most influential newspaper Babel which does not appear on Fridays.
Uday holds a degree in engineering and military studies. He was also chairman of Iraq's Union of Journalists for two sessions.

Two years ago he supervised a national drive to repair and maintain a great number of Iraqi helicopter gunships, tanks and armoured personnel carriers. He also set up a new force known as "Saddam Commandos".
President Saddam Hussein has two sons and three daughters.
